title: Saraswati, the River
hookLine: before she held a veena, Saraswati was a river the Rig Veda called best of mothers
carry: knowledge is sacred: saraswati flows through it
tomorrow: saraswati takes hold of a giant's tongue

lines: A GODDESS IN WHITE WITH A VEENA.
cards: Where does a goddess of learning come from? The familiar image is calm and bright: a woman in white, seated by water, a veena in her hands, a book, a string of beads, a swan nearby.

Some students bow to her before exams; some musicians touch her picture before they play. But in the Rig Veda her story isn't a woman with a book at all. It's water, moving fast, carving through hills.
Today's character is Saraswati, and she starts out as a river.

teach.h: IN THE RIG VEDA, A RUSHING RIVER.
teach.b: In the Rig Veda, Sarasvati is a river, and the hymns don't treat her as a gentle one. One hymn has her bursting through the ridges of the hills with her strong waves, the way someone digging pulls up lotus roots.
She's loud, she's powerful, and she nourishes the people along her banks.

One verse gives her a triple praise that's hard to forget: best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses. In Sanskrit it rings: ambitame, naditame, devitame. Mother, river, goddess, in one breath.

teach.h: THE RIVER BECOMES SPEECH AND LEARNING.
teach.b: Over the long life of the tradition, the river becomes the goddess of speech, learning, music and wisdom. Some later texts link her with Vak, sacred speech itself.
So the one who flowed now flows another way: through words, through a song, through a mind finally understanding something. Tradition also says the river didn't simply vanish.
Pilgrims at Prayag, where the Ganga and the Yamuna meet, speak of a third river joining them there, hidden underground: Sarasvati, unseen but present.
So here is the teaching: in Hinduism, knowledge itself is sacred. Learning isn't only a skill; it's a goddess's flow.

That's why, on Vasant Panchami, students set books and instruments before her image, and why so many Hindu kids, if a foot touches a book, touch the book and then their forehead: a small apology to Saraswati.

how: Saraswati is honored by students, teachers and musicians; on Vasant Panchami in spring, some families and schools place books, pens and instruments before her image and leave them there for the day.

o: a hidden third river that meets at Prayag
the warrior Goddess, first of five met as characters
a river goddess praised in the old Rig Veda

games.q: Saraswati, from river to learning: tap the pairs.

s: in the Rig Veda, Sarasvati is a quiet stream
one hymn has her bursting through the ridges of the hills with her strong waves.
one Rig Veda verse calls her best of mothers, rivers and goddesses
Saraswati was a goddess of learning from her very first appearance
in the Rig Veda she's above all a river; later tradition makes her the goddess of speech and learning.

games.q: you're a pilgrim at Prayag, where two rivers you can see meet. what does tradition tell you is also there?
o: Sarasvati, a third river, hidden underground
games.why: tradition says the Sarasvati joins the Ganga and Yamuna there unseen, which is why the meeting is called a meeting of three.

practice: Pick up a book, a notebook, an instrument, whatever you're learning with, and touch it to your forehead, the small bow Hindu kids give a book.

Then notice that most of your learning happens where you can't see it, like the river underground, and let that be all right. If you pray, bow inwardly to Saraswati; if you don't, bow to what you're learning.

wordCard.voice: Durga. The name at the head of this run; today, it opens onto Saraswati, the river who became the goddess of learning. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Sarasvati, first a river in the Rig Veda, later the goddess of speech, learning and music.
